```{r}
#| label: setup
library(mizer)
library(ggplot2)
options(mizer_info_level = 0)
source("R/build_model.R")
source("R/combined_model.R")
source("R/background_model.R")

# Results of the scripts in background/
res <- readRDS("background/scan.rds")
scan <- res$scan
cases <- readRDS("background/cases.rds")
fishing <- readRDS("background/fishing.rds")

col_species <- c(Sprat = "#2a78d6", Cod = "#eb6834")
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
              theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
                    legend.position = "top",
                    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0)))
fmt <- function(x, digits = 2) format(signif(x, digits), big.mark = ",",
                                      scientific = FALSE, trim = TRUE)
#' A biomass relative to the coexistence state, as text
biomass_text <- function(x, alive = 1e-3) {
    ifelse(x < alive, "dies out",
           ifelse(x > 1e3, "> 1000×", sprintf("%.2f×", x)))
}
#' "min–max" of x with a fixed number of decimals
range_text <- function(x, decimals = 2) {
    paste(sprintf(paste0("%.", decimals, "f"), range(x)), collapse = "–")
}
#' The scan result at one grid point
at <- function(phi_prey, phi_larv, cod_resource) {
    scan[abs(scan$phi_prey - phi_prey) < 1e-9 &
             abs(scan$phi_larv - phi_larv) < 1e-9 &
             scan$cod_resource == cod_resource, ]
}
variant_label <- function(cod_resource) {
    factor(ifelse(cod_resource, "Cod larvae eat plankton",
                  "Cod larvae eat background food only"),
           levels = c("Cod larvae eat background food only",
                      "Cod larvae eat plankton"))
}
scan$variant <- variant_label(scan$cod_resource)
```

```{r}
#| label: classify
# What happens at each point of the scan
#   barrier    a rare cod cannot invade the cod-free state
#   unstable   the coexistence state has an eigenvalue with a positive real
#              part (well above rounding error)
#   cycles     cod started 20 % above the coexistence state still vary by
#              more than 5 % over the last 100 of 1000 years
#   dying      cod started 20 % above it are below 1 % of it after 1000
#              years. At one point they are then still at 0.5 % and falling;
#              a longer run in background/run_cases.R shows them dying out.
scan$barrier <- scan$R0 < 0.999
scan$unstable <- scan$lead_re > 1e-6
scan$cycles <- scan$above_cod_max > 1.05 * scan$above_cod_min
scan$dying <- scan$above_cod < 0.01
alive <- 1e-3
regimes <- c("No barrier: cod invade",
             "Barrier. Coexistence state stable",
             "Barrier. Threshold: cod settle above it",
             "Barrier. Threshold: cod cycle above it",
             "Barrier. Cod die out from above and below")
scan$regime <- factor(regimes[with(scan, ifelse(
    !barrier, 1, ifelse(
        !unstable, 2, ifelse(
            dying, 5, ifelse(cycles, 4, 3)))))],
    levels = regimes)
n_regime <- function(k, cod_resource = c(TRUE, FALSE)) {
    sum(scan$regime %in% regimes[k] & scan$cod_resource %in% cod_resource)
}
# The points at which cod hold sprat down
on <- scan[scan$phi_prey > 0, ]
# The cod states above the threshold, where cod have clearly left it
strong_above <- scan[scan$regime == regimes[3] & scan$above_cod > 1.05, ]
```

```{r}
#| label: numbers
# The coexistence state with both links close to their largest strength
p_max <- new_background_params(phi_prey = 0.96, phi_larv = 0.96)
shares <- background_shares(p_max)
theta_max <- other_params(p_max)$background$theta_max
sp_max <- as.data.frame(species_params(p_max))
dlnw <- log(w(p_max)[2] / w(p_max)[1])
#' Size at which a share is largest
w_peak <- function(x) w(p_max)[which.max(x)]
#' Share at the size class nearest to w
share_at <- function(x, w0) x[which.min(abs(w(p_max) - w0))]
# Who eats the background prey, and what stays fixed
prey_mort <- background_prey_mort(p_max)
sprat_prey_share <- prey_mort["Sprat", ] / colSums(prey_mort)
#' Value of x at the size of the resource spectrum nearest to w0
at_prey <- function(x, w0) x[which.min(abs(w_full(p_max) - w0))]
fixed_share <- ext_encounter(p_max) / getEncounter(p_max)
# With cod larvae eating background food only
p_larval <- new_background_params(phi_prey = 0.96, phi_larv = 0.96,
                                  cod_resource = FALSE)
fixed_larval <- (ext_encounter(p_larval) / getEncounter(p_larval))["Cod", ]
level <- other_params(p_max)$background$background_level
# The same state with the links at half strength: every rate is the same
p_half <- new_background_params(phi_prey = 0.48, phi_larv = 0.48)
# (at the sizes at which the species occur)
present <- initialN(p_max) > 0
same_rates <- max(abs(getEGrowth(p_half) / getEGrowth(p_max) - 1)[present],
                  abs(getMort(p_half) / getMort(p_max) - 1)[present],
                  na.rm = TRUE)

sens <- cases$sensitivity
intro <- cases$intro
pts <- cases$points
# The two slow points of the scan. Cycle: troughs of cod after the transient
slow <- cases$slow
slow_cycle <- slow[slow$phi_prey == 0.36 & slow$factor == 1.2 &
                       slow$time > 300, ]
slow_troughs <- slow_cycle$time[which(diff(sign(diff(slow_cycle$cod))) == 2) + 1]
slow_period <- diff(slow_troughs)[1]
# Scan results at the four points
pt <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(pts)), function(i) {
    at(pts$phi_prey[i], pts$phi_larv[i], pts$cod_resource[i])
})

# Fishing
fb <- fishing$branches
fb$sweep <- factor(fb$sweep, levels = fishing$sweeps)
fb$case <- factor(fb$case, levels = fishing$cases$label)
abundant <- 0.1
up <- fb[fb$sweep == fishing$sweeps[1], ]
up1 <- up[up$case == fishing$cases$label[1], ]
up2 <- up[up$case == fishing$cases$label[2], ]
# Without a barrier the runs settle very slowly near the fishing mortality
# at which cod vanish. Only the settled steps are used.
up3 <- up[up$case == fishing$cases$label[3] & up$converged, ]
down <- fb[fb$sweep == fishing$sweeps[2], ]
down3 <- down[down$case == fishing$cases$label[3] & down$converged, ]
#' Last fishing mortality with cod above `floor`, and the first without
last_F <- function(d, floor = abundant) max(d$F_cod[d$Cod > floor])
collapse_F <- function(d, floor = abundant) {
    min(d$F_cod[d$F_cod > last_F(d, floor)])
}
#' Cod biomass on a branch at one fishing mortality
cod_at <- function(d, F_cod) d$Cod[abs(d$F_cod - F_cod) < 1e-9]
# Without a barrier: how far the two sweeps are apart
sweep_gap <- max(abs(down3$Cod[match(up3$F_cod, down3$F_cod)] - up3$Cod),
                 na.rm = TRUE)
unsettled <- up$F_cod[up$case == fishing$cases$label[3] & !up$converged]
sf <- fishing$sprat_fishery
sf1 <- sf[sf$case == fishing$cases$label[1], ]
sf2 <- sf[sf$case == fishing$cases$label[2], ]
sf3 <- sf[sf$case == fishing$cases$label[3], ]
# Natural mortality of cod at the third point
p_open <- new_background_params(pts$phi_prey[3], pts$phi_larv[3],
                                pts$cod_resource[3])
cod_mort <- function(w0) getMort(p_open)["Cod", which.min(abs(w(p_open) - w0))]
```

# Summary

The [combined model](combined_model.html) showed two mechanisms that can keep
a collapsed cod stock from recovering: the emergent Allee effect of
@vanleeuwen2008, in which a rare cod finds too little sprat to eat, and
cultivation–depensation [@walters2001cultivation], in which abundant sprat eat
cod eggs and larvae. In that model cod, sprat and plankton are the whole
community.

Here the two species are embedded in a **power-law background**. In the
coexistence state every fish meets food and dies at power-law rates, as in a
community with a Sheldon spectrum. Only part of those rates comes from the
other species and from the plankton. The rest is the background:

* a **background mortality**, which is fixed;
* **background prey**, which cod and sprat eat down and which recovers when
  they eat less, as the plankton does.

Two parameters, `phi_prey` and `phi_larv`, set how much of the power-law
rates the two predation links account for, from none (0) to as much as they
can (1).

The main results:

* **Cultivation–depensation persists.** Sprat predation on cod larvae lowers
  the invasion fitness $R_0$ of cod in the cod-free state by a factor of up
  to `r fmt(1 / min(scan$larval_predation), 2)`.
* **The mechanism of Van Leeuwen et al. does not.** Sprat as food *raise*
  $R_0$ in the cod-free state, by a factor of up to
  `r fmt(max(scan$prey), 2)`. In a power-law background, cod depend on sprat
  only at 30 g to 1 kg, when they eat adult sprat, and there are more adult
  sprat without cod.
* **Competition takes its place.** If cod larvae eat plankton, the more
  numerous sprat leave them less. That lowers $R_0$ by a factor of up to
  `r fmt(1 / min(scan$competition), 2)`. Sprat also graze down the small
  background prey that juvenile cod eat.
* **The background prey works against every barrier.** A rare cod has to
  itself the background prey that the cod of the coexistence state eat down.
  That raises $R_0$ by a factor of `r range_text(scan$background, 1)`. The
  cod-free state is closed only where the links are strong: at
  `r n_regime(2:5)` of the `r nrow(scan)` points of the scan. With both links
  at half strength, $R_0$ is `r fmt(at(0.48, 0.48, FALSE)$R0, 2)` without
  and `r fmt(at(0.48, 0.48, TRUE)$R0, 2)` with competition for plankton.
* **Cod limit themselves.** More cod leave less background prey. Where cod
  can invade, the coexistence state is stable and is the only cod state. In
  no run do cod take over or grow without bound.
* **Behind a barrier the coexistence state is mostly the Allee threshold.**
  It is stable at only `r n_regime(2)` of the `r n_regime(2:5)` points with a
  barrier. At the others cod started below it die out. Cod started above it
  settle at a state with more cod and fewer sprat, cycle, or at the
  strongest links die out too.
* **The cod states withstand very little cod fishing.** Behind a barrier
  they collapse at a fishing mortality of `r collapse_F(up1)`/yr and
  `r collapse_F(up2)`/yr, and cod do not return when fishing stops. Without
  a barrier cod decline steadily and are gone at
  `r collapse_F(up3, alive)`/yr. The combined model's cod state persisted up
  to 0.27/yr.
* **A sprat fishery opens the way back.** It lets cod invade the cod-free
  state from a sprat fishing mortality of
  `r min(sf2$F_sprat[sf2$R0 > 1])`–`r min(sf1$F_sprat[sf1$R0 > 1])`/yr at the
  two points with a barrier that were tried.
* **How far the background prey gives way is a free choice, and it
  matters.** At one point of the scan, $R_0$ is
  `r fmt(sens$R0[sens$variant == "Background level 0.2"], 2)` if the prey
  sits at 0.2 of its carrying capacity,
  `r fmt(sens$R0[sens$variant == "Baseline"], 2)` at the default of 0.5, and
  `r fmt(sens$R0[sens$variant == "Fixed background"], 2)` if the background
  is fixed.

# The model {#model}

## A background

In the [cod–sprat model](index.html) and in the
[combined model](combined_model.html), cod, sprat and plankton are the whole
community. All sprat mortality above 0.01 g is cod predation or a constant,
and cod above the diet-shift size eat sprat or starve. Real cod and sprat
have many other predators and prey. Those soften every feedback between the
two species.

Here the two species live in a community that is not modelled. In the
coexistence state every individual

* meets food at a rate proportional to $w^n$, with $n = 0.7$, and
* dies at a rate proportional to $w^{n-1}$,

as it would in a community with a Sheldon spectrum. Only part of that food
and of that mortality comes from the modelled species and from the plankton.
The rest is the **background**:

* **Background mortality** is fixed. It does not change when cod or sprat
  do.
* **Background prey** stands for the other animals that cod and sprat eat.
  It is depleted by what they eat of it and recovers when they eat less, as
  the plankton does.

## Construction

`new_background_params()` in `R/background_model.R` builds the model with the
allometric workflow of the mizerEcopath package:

1. **`newAllometricParams()`** sets up cod and sprat without any interaction.
   Each species has a power-law encounter rate, chosen to give its age at
   maturity, and a power-law mortality, chosen so that the juvenile biomass
   density falls as $w^{-0.2}$. There is no satiation and no metabolic loss.
   The species are in steady state, with the biomasses of the cod state of the
   [cod–sprat model](index.html).
2. **`setFeedingLevels()`** introduces satiation and metabolism: a feeding
   level of 0.6 and a critical feeding level of 0.2 at all sizes. It raises
   the encounter rate so that growth is unchanged. From here on the species
   respond to a change in food.
3. **`makeInteracting()`** switches on two predation links: cod eat sprat, and
   sprat eat cod eggs and larvae. Whatever predation this creates is
   subtracted from the external encounter and the external mortality.
4. **`setResourceInteraction()`** lets the species feed on a dynamic plankton
   resource, a power law up to 0.1 g. Feeding on plankton replaces as much of
   the external encounter as it can. The plankton is a semichemostat at half
   its carrying capacity.

5. **`set_background_response()`**, in `R/background_model.R`, turns the
   external encounter that is left into feeding on background prey
   (@sec-prey).

Steps 2–5 move food and mortality from the background to the modelled world
but do not change any rate. So the coexistence state is the **same steady
state for every strength of the links**: with the links at half strength,
growth and mortality differ from those at nearly full strength only by
rounding error (a relative difference below $10^{`r ceiling(log10(same_rates))`}$). The combined model had to recalibrate `erepro` at every point to
hold its cod state fixed. Here that comes for free.

Life histories are those of the earlier models (sprat to 15 g, cod to 10 kg,
predator–prey mass ratios of 1000 and 30). Both species enter as 1 mg eggs,
and there is no imposed stock–recruitment relation (`R_max = Inf`).

## The two links

The strength of each link is a fraction φ of the largest strength for which
the background stays non-negative:

* **`phi_prey`**: cod eating sprat. At 1, the cod that depend most on sprat
  get all their food from sprat.
* **`phi_larv`**: sprat eating cod eggs and larvae. At 1, the cod that sprat
  eat most die only from sprat predation.

At 0 a link is absent and its share stays in the background. φ is therefore
a measure of how little the background dilutes a link.

## The background prey {#sec-prey}

The background prey is a second spectrum of food next to the plankton:

* **What it is.** The power law of the plankton, continued from the largest
  plankton size of 0.1 g up to the size of the largest cod.
* **Who eats it.** Both species, through their predation kernels. Each
  predator finds it with an availability that depends on its own size. The
  availability is chosen so that the predator's encounter rate in the
  coexistence state does not change.
* **How it responds.** Each size class is a semichemostat, like the
  plankton. In the coexistence state it sits at a **background level** of
  `r level`: that fraction of its carrying capacity. If the predation on a
  size class changes by a factor $x$, its abundance settles at
  $1 / (\lambda + (1 - \lambda) x)$ of what it was, with $\lambda$ the
  background level.
  * Prey that is no longer eaten rises by a factor of `r fmt(1 / level, 2)`.
  * Prey that is eaten twice as much falls to
    `r fmt(1 / (level + (1 - level) * 2), 2)`.
  * At a level of 1 the background food is fixed.
* **What stays fixed.** External food responds only as far as a Sheldon
  spectrum would supply it from prey above 0.1 g. Small larvae could reach
  such prey only with the tail of their kernel.
  * With cod larvae eating plankton, at most
    `r fmt(100 * max(fixed_share["Cod", ]), 1)` % of the food of cod stays
    fixed.
  * With cod larvae eating background food only, their food is fixed up to
    0.1 g, and `r fmt(100 * share_at(fixed_larval, 1), 2)` % fixed at 1 g
    and `r fmt(100 * share_at(fixed_larval, 10), 1)` % at 10 g.

The background prey is held in mizer's resource spectrum, above the plankton.
So `getStability()`, the Newton solver and `cod_R0()` treat it as part of the
state, as they do the plankton.

```{r}
#| label: fig-shares
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| fig-cap: "What the modelled world accounts for in the coexistence state, with both links at φ = 0.96 and cod larvae feeding on plankton. Left: shares of the food of cod. Right: shares of the mortality of each species. The remainder of the mortality is the fixed background."
share_data <- rbind(
    data.frame(panel = "Food of cod", w = w(p_max),
               share = shares$prey["Cod", ], what = "Sprat"),
    data.frame(panel = "Food of cod", w = w(p_max),
               share = shares$resource["Cod", ], what = "Plankton"),
    data.frame(panel = "Food of cod", w = w(p_max),
               share = shares$background["Cod", ], what = "Background prey"),
    data.frame(panel = "Mortality", w = w(p_max),
               share = shares$predation["Cod", ],
               what = "Cod eaten by sprat"),
    data.frame(panel = "Mortality", w = w(p_max)[present["Sprat", ]],
               share = shares$predation["Sprat", present["Sprat", ]],
               what = "Sprat eaten by cod"))
share_data$what <- factor(share_data$what, levels = unique(share_data$what))
ggplot(share_data, aes(w, share, colour = what)) +
    geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
    facet_wrap(~panel) +
    scale_x_log10(breaks = 10^(-3:4),
                  labels = c("0.001", "0.01", "0.1", "1", "10", "100",
                             "1000", "10000")) +
    scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1), labels = scales::percent) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c("#2a78d6", "#1baf7a", "#8a5cc7", "#eda100",
                                   "#eb6834"), name = NULL) +
    labs(x = "Body weight (g)", y = "Share of the power-law rate") +
    guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 2))
```

@fig-shares shows what the links can account for at most. The pattern follows
from the shapes of the spectra. The abundance of one species falls as
$w^{-1.2}$ among its juveniles. The community that the power-law rates stand
for falls as $w^{-2.05}$. A species therefore matters to others mainly **near
its own largest sizes**:

* **Sprat as food.** Cod of about `r fmt(w_peak(shares$prey["Cod", ]), 1)` g,
  which eat adult sprat, can get
  `r fmt(100 * max(shares$prey["Cod", ]), 2)` % of their food from sprat. Cod
  of 1 g get `r fmt(100 * share_at(shares$prey["Cod", ], 1), 1)` %, and cod
  of 0.1 g `r fmt(100 * share_at(shares$prey["Cod", ], 0.1), 1)` %. The small
  sprat that small cod eat are a negligible part of the food at that size.
* **Cod as predators.** Cod cause up to
  `r fmt(100 * max(shares$predation["Sprat", present["Sprat", ]]), 2)` % of the
  mortality of the largest sprat, but only
  `r fmt(100 * share_at(shares$predation["Sprat", ], 0.1), 1)` % of that of
  0.1 g sprat.
* **Sprat as predators.** Adult sprat can cause
  `r fmt(100 * max(shares$predation["Cod", ]), 2)` % of the mortality of cod
  larvae of `r fmt(w_peak(shares$predation["Cod", ]), 1)` g, and
  `r fmt(100 * share_at(shares$predation["Cod", ], 0.001), 2)` % of that of
  eggs.
* **Plankton.** Sprat get nearly all their food from plankton
  (`r fmt(100 * min(shares$resource["Sprat", present["Sprat", ]]), 2)` % or
  more), which is what regulates them. Cod larvae up to 0.1 g can get
  `r fmt(100 * share_at(shares$resource["Cod", ], 0.01), 3)` % of theirs from
  plankton, and then compete with sprat.
* **Background prey.** It is the rest of the food of cod above 0.1 g:
  `r fmt(100 * share_at(shares$background["Cod", ], 10), 2)` % at 10 g,
  `r fmt(100 * share_at(shares$background["Cod", ], 300), 2)` % at 300 g,
  where cod eat most sprat, and
  `r fmt(100 * share_at(shares$background["Cod", ], 3000), 2)` % at 3 kg.
  Sprat take at most
  `r fmt(100 * max(shares$background["Sprat", present["Sprat", ]]), 2)` % of
  their food from it. But sprat are many, so they cause
  `r fmt(100 * at_prey(sprat_prey_share, 0.15), 2)` % of the mortality of
  background prey of 0.15 g and
  `r fmt(100 * at_prey(sprat_prey_share, 1), 2)` % of that of 1 g. Above 10 g
  only cod eat it. Juvenile cod of 0.3 to 30 g therefore share their
  background prey with sprat.

This already bears on the two mechanisms. Cultivation–depensation needs adult
forage fish to eat the young of their predator, which the embedding allows at
almost full strength. The mechanism of @vanleeuwen2008 needs juvenile cod to
depend on small sprat, which it does not allow: in a power-law background the
dependence of cod on sprat lies with cod of 30 g to 1 kg that eat adult sprat.

## Cod larvae and plankton

`setResourceInteraction()` moves food from the background to the plankton for
both species. Cod larvae then share their food with sprat. The combined model
deliberately kept this competition out by giving cod larvae a fixed food. Both
variants are studied here:

* **Cod larvae eat plankton** (`cod_resource = TRUE`): the workflow as it
  stands.
* **Cod larvae eat background food only** (`cod_resource = FALSE`): the
  plankton share of the cod diet is handed back to the background, where it
  is a fixed food (@sec-prey). This is the closer analogue of the combined
  model.

## Numerics

The model uses mizer's first-order upwind scheme without size diffusion, as
the workflow produces it and as in the [cod–sprat model](index.html), on
`r length(w(p_max))` size classes ($\Delta \ln w = `r fmt(dlnw, 2)`$). The
combined model's second-order scheme with size diffusion was not carried over:
with diffusion, `steadySingleSpecies()` leaves an unbalanced diffusive flux
out of the largest size class of each species. The combined model avoided
that with a senescence mortality, which would break the power law.

Steady states other than the coexistence state are found by projection, with
Euler steps of 0.1 yr. $R_0$ comes from `cod_R0()` of the combined model,
which solves the discretised transport equation and is exact for this scheme.

# Telling the mechanisms apart

As in the combined model, the invasion fitness $R_0$ of a rare cod in the
cod-free state is decomposed by taking one thing from the cod-free state and
the rest from the coexistence state, where $R_0 = 1$:

* **Prey**: the sprat that cod eat. This is the route of @vanleeuwen2008. It
  is below 1 if cod find less sprat to eat without cod.
* **Competition**: the plankton that cod eat. It is below 1 if the more
  numerous sprat leave less plankton for cod larvae. This route is absent
  when cod larvae eat background food only.
* **Background**: the background prey that cod eat. Two things pull it in
  opposite directions. The prey that only cod ate recovers without cod, which
  raises it. The more numerous sprat graze down the small background prey
  that juvenile cod eat, which lowers it.
* **Food**: all three together, that is the growth and reproduction of cod.
* **Larval predation**: the mortality of cod. This is
  cultivation–depensation.
* **Interaction** = $R_0$ / (food × larval predation). It is below 1 if hungry
  cod linger at the sizes at which sprat eat them.

$R_0 < 1$ means that cod cannot invade the cod-free state. In the combined
model that implied two alternative stable states, because the cod state was
stable. Here the coexistence state need not be stable, so its stability is
checked separately: from the leading eigenvalue of `getStability()`, and by
starting cod 20 % below and 20 % above it.

# Results

## The cod-free state

Removing cod takes away part of the mortality of sprat, mostly that of the
adults (@fig-shares), and all the mortality of the background prey that only
cod eat. Sprat biomass then rises by a factor of
`r range_text(on$sprat_free)`, depending on `phi_prey` only. The plankton
that sprat graze falls, and with it the feeding level of sprat.

```{r}
#| label: fig-spectra
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-cap: "The cod-free state relative to the coexistence state at the four points of @tbl-points: abundance of sprat, of plankton and of background prey by size. Without cod there are more sprat. They graze down the plankton and the small background prey, and the large background prey recovers. The first and last points have the same prey link, so their curves nearly coincide."
spec <- cases$spectra[cases$spectra$what != "Sprat feeding level", ]
spec$point <- factor(spec$point, levels = pts$label)
spec$what <- factor(spec$what, levels = c("Sprat", "Plankton",
                                          "Background prey"))
# The largest background prey is eaten by no one and does not change
w_eaten <- max(w_full(p_max)[colSums(prey_mort) > 0])
spec <- spec[spec$what != "Background prey" | spec$w <= w_eaten, ]
ggplot(spec[spec$w >= 1e-6, ], aes(w, ratio, colour = point)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 1, colour = "grey45", linetype = "dashed") +
    geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
    facet_wrap(~what, scales = "free_x") +
    scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_log()) +
    scale_y_log10() +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c("#2a78d6", "#1baf7a", "#eda100",
                                   "#eb6834"), name = NULL) +
    labs(x = "Body weight (g)",
         y = "Abundance without cod /\nabundance in the coexistence state") +
    guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 2)) +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r}
#| label: spectra-numbers
spectra <- cases$spectra
#' A column of the spectra at point i, at the size nearest to w0
spec_at <- function(i, what, w0) {
    d <- spectra[spectra$point == pts$label[i] & spectra$what == what, ]
    d$ratio[which.min(abs(log(d$w / w0)))]
}
```

Three things in @fig-spectra matter for what follows:

* **There are more sprat of every size.** At the first point, with the
  strongest prey link, the largest sprat (14 g) are
  `r fmt(spec_at(1, "Sprat", 14), 2)` times as abundant without cod, because
  cod no longer eat them. They lay more eggs, so the smallest sprat (1 mg)
  are `r fmt(spec_at(1, "Sprat", 0.001), 2)` times as abundant. Sprat of 1 g
  are `r fmt(spec_at(1, "Sprat", 1), 3)` times as abundant. No size that cod
  eat becomes scarcer. In the model of @vanleeuwen2008 it is the other way
  round: without cod, sprat produce *fewer* young.
* **Sprat do not become stunted.** Their feeding level falls from 0.6 to
  `r fmt(spec_at(1, "Sprat feeding level", 10), 2)` at 10 g, far above the
  critical feeding level of 0.2. The plankton sits at half its carrying
  capacity in the coexistence state, so it gives way only so far: it falls to
  `r fmt(spec_at(1, "Plankton", 0.01), 2)` of its abundance at 0.01 g. In the
  [cod–sprat model](index.html), adult sprat fed at 0.34 with cod and at
  0.18–0.20, their starvation level, without.
* **The background prey moves both ways.**
  * Prey above about 10 g, which only cod eat, rises to its carrying
    capacity: `r fmt(spec_at(1, "Background prey", 100), 2)` times its
    abundance with cod, at every point.
  * The smallest background prey falls, because sprat eat most of it and
    there are more sprat. At the first point it falls to
    `r fmt(spec_at(1, "Background prey", 0.15), 2)` of its abundance at
    0.15 g and to `r fmt(spec_at(1, "Background prey", 1), 2)` at 1 g. This
    is a second route of competition, and it is there whether or not cod
    larvae eat plankton.

## The regime map

```{r}
#| label: fig-regime
#| fig-height: 6.5
#| fig-cap: "$R_0$ of a rare cod in the cod-free state over the strengths of the two links. The black line is $R_0 = 1$: above and to the right of it cod cannot invade. The symbols show what the coexistence state is (see text)."
map <- scan
map$log_R0 <- pmin(pmax(log10(map$R0), -2), 0.5)
ggplot(map, aes(phi_prey, phi_larv)) +
    geom_raster(aes(fill = log_R0)) +
    geom_contour(aes(z = log_R0), breaks = 0, colour = "black",
                 linewidth = 0.9) +
    geom_point(aes(shape = regime), size = 2.2) +
    facet_wrap(~variant) +
    scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2a78d6", mid = "white", high = "#eb6834",
                         midpoint = 0, limits = c(-2, 0.5),
                         breaks = c(-2, -1, 0, 0.5),
                         labels = c("≤ 0.01", "0.1", "1", "3"),
                         name = expression(R[0] ~ "of cod in the cod-free state")) +
    scale_shape_manual(values = c(1, 16, 17, 15, 4), name = NULL, drop = FALSE) +
    scale_x_continuous(expand = c(0, 0), breaks = seq(0, 0.96, by = 0.24)) +
    scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0, 0), breaks = seq(0, 0.96, by = 0.24)) +
    labs(x = "Cod eating sprat, φ_prey",
         y = "Sprat eating cod larvae, φ_larv") +
    guides(fill = guide_colourbar(order = 1),
           shape = guide_legend(order = 2, ncol = 1)) +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.box = "vertical",
          legend.key.width = unit(1.5, "cm"), panel.spacing = unit(1, "lines"))
```

@fig-regime shows the invasion fitness of cod in the cod-free state and, as
symbols, what the coexistence state is.

**Can cod invade?** Without cod, the background prey that cod had eaten down
recovers. Where cod do not eat sprat (`phi_prey` = 0) hardly anything else
changes, and $R_0$ is `r fmt(max(scan$R0), 3)`: a rare cod finds more food than the
cod of the coexistence state, and cod return to that state. Every barrier has
to overcome this head start. It needs `phi_prey` > 0, because only then are
there more sprat without cod.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-barrier
#| tbl-cap: "The strength `phi_larv` of sprat predation on cod larvae from which cod cannot invade the cod-free state, by the strength `phi_prey` of cod predation on sprat. It is interpolated between the points of the scan."
barrier_from <- function(cod_resource) {
    d <- scan[scan$cod_resource == cod_resource, ]
    sapply(sort(unique(d$phi_prey)), function(pp) {
        k <- d[abs(d$phi_prey - pp) < 1e-9, ]
        if (all(k$barrier)) return("always")
        if (!any(k$barrier)) return("never")
        sprintf("%.2f", approx(k$R0, k$phi_larv, xout = 1)$y)
    })
}
barrier_table <- rbind(barrier_from(FALSE), barrier_from(TRUE))
colnames(barrier_table) <- sprintf("%.2f", sort(unique(scan$phi_prey)))
knitr::kable(data.frame(
    `φ_prey` = c("Cod larvae eat background food only",
                 "Cod larvae eat plankton"),
    barrier_table, check.names = FALSE), align = "lrrrrrrrrr")
```

* **Cod larvae eat background food only** (left). Larval predation is the
  only barrier. It closes the cod-free state at
  `r n_regime(2:5, FALSE)` of the `r sum(!scan$cod_resource)` points, where
  both links are strong (@tbl-barrier). At the strongest links $R_0$ is
  `r fmt(at(0.96, 0.96, FALSE)$R0, 2)`.
* **Cod larvae eat plankton** (right). Competition adds to larval predation,
  and the cod-free state is closed at `r n_regime(2:5, TRUE)` points. From a
  `phi_prey` of 0.84 it is closed even without larval predation ($R_0$ =
  `r fmt(at(0.84, 0, TRUE)$R0, 2)` and `r fmt(at(0.96, 0, TRUE)$R0, 2)`). At
  the strongest links $R_0$ is `r fmt(at(0.96, 0.96, TRUE)$R0, 2)`.

**What is the coexistence state?**

* **The only cod state** (○) wherever cod can invade. It is then stable,
  with one exception (below), and cod started 20 % below or above it return
  to it. Close to the line $R_0 = 1$ they return very slowly.
* **A stable cod state behind a barrier** (●) at `r n_regime(2, FALSE)` of
  the `r n_regime(2:5, FALSE)` points with a barrier on the left, and at
  `r n_regime(2, TRUE)` of `r n_regime(2:5, TRUE)` on the right. They lie in
  a narrow band next to the line $R_0 = 1$. Only there is this model
  bistable in the way the combined model was. Even then the basin can be
  small: at `r sum(scan$regime == regimes[2] & scan$below_cod < 0.5)` of
  these points, cod started 20 % below the state die out.
* **The Allee threshold** (▲, ■) at most points with a barrier. The state has
  a real positive eigenvalue, of up to
  `r fmt(max(scan$lead_re), 2)`/yr. Cod started 20 % below it die out. Cod
  started 20 % above it
  * settle at a state with more cod and fewer sprat (▲). That state is the
    cod state there. It has `r range_text(strong_above$above_cod)` times the
    cod and `r range_text(strong_above$above_sprat)` times the sprat of the
    coexistence state;
  * or cycle (■), at `r n_regime(4)` points with strong links. Cod then
    vary by up to a factor of
    `r fmt(max((scan$above_cod_max / scan$above_cod_min)[scan$regime == regimes[4]]), 2)`
    within 100 years.
* **An unstable state that cod cannot hold from either side** (×), at
  `r n_regime(5)` points, most of them at the strongest links. Cod started
  above it die out as well.

**Two points are slow.** Both were followed for
`r max(slow$time)` years (`background/run_cases.R`):

* **A slow cycle where cod can invade.** At `phi_prey` = 0.36 and
  `phi_larv` = 0.72, with cod larvae eating plankton, $R_0$ is
  `r fmt(at(0.36, 0.72, TRUE)$R0, 3)` and the coexistence state is unstable,
  with a growth rate of `r fmt(at(0.36, 0.72, TRUE)$lead_re, 1)`/yr. Cod
  cycle between `r fmt(min(slow_cycle$cod), 2)` and
  `r fmt(max(slow_cycle$cod), 2)` times their coexistence biomass, with a
  period of about `r fmt(slow_period, 2)` years.
* **A slow death.** At `phi_prey` = 0.6 and `phi_larv` = 0.24, with cod
  larvae eating plankton, the leading eigenvalues are a complex pair with a
  real part of `r fmt(at(0.6, 0.24, TRUE)$lead_re, 1)`/yr. Cod started 20 %
  above the state return to it, pass it and die out. They are still at
  `r fmt(100 * at(0.6, 0.24, TRUE)$above_cod, 1)` % of it after 1000 years.

**Cod limit themselves.** In no run do cod take over, and in none do they
grow without bound: the largest cod biomass that any run from above reaches
is `r fmt(max(scan$above_cod_max), 2)` times that of the coexistence state,
and sprat never fall below `r fmt(min(scan$above_sprat[scan$above_cod > alive]), 2)`
of theirs. The background prey gives way under more cod.

**Why is the coexistence state unstable where there is a barrier?** With
`R_max = Inf`, cod are regulated only through what they do to their food and
to sprat. More cod mean less background prey and fewer sprat, and that has
four effects on cod:

* less background prey to eat, which stabilises;
* less sprat to eat, which stabilises;
* fewer larvae eaten, which destabilises;
* more plankton for cod larvae, which destabilises.

The last two are the mechanisms that close the cod-free state. Where they are
strong enough to do that against the head start that the background prey
gives a rare cod, they are mostly also strong enough to outweigh the first
two at the coexistence state. So the line $R_0 = 1$ and the edge of
stability lie close together in @fig-regime, with the bistable band between
them.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-points
#| tbl-cap: "Four points of the regime map. The factors of $R_0$ are explained in the previous section. The last two columns give cod and sprat biomass, relative to the coexistence state, 1000 years after cod are started 20 % above it. A range is that of the last 100 years."
#' Biomass after the run from above: a range where it still varies
above_text <- function(lo, hi) {
    ifelse(hi > 1.05 * lo & hi > alive,
           sprintf("%.2f–%.2f×", lo, hi), biomass_text(hi))
}
# Sprat over the last 100 years of the runs from above in background/cases.rds
sprat_above <- lapply(pts$label, function(l) {
    d <- cases$departures
    d$sprat[d$point == l & d$factor > 1 & d$time > max(d$time) - 100]
})
knitr::kable(data.frame(
    Point = pts$label,
    φ_prey = pts$phi_prey,
    φ_larv = pts$phi_larv,
    `Cod larvae eat plankton` = ifelse(pts$cod_resource, "yes", "no"),
    Prey = sprintf("%.2f", sapply(pt, `[[`, "prey")),
    Competition = sprintf("%.2f", sapply(pt, `[[`, "competition")),
    Background = sprintf("%.2f", sapply(pt, `[[`, "background")),
    `Larval predation` = sprintf("%.2f", sapply(pt, `[[`, "larval_predation")),
    R0 = sprintf("**%.2f**", sapply(pt, `[[`, "R0")),
    `Growth rate of the instability (1/yr)` = ifelse(
        sapply(pt, `[[`, "unstable"),
        sprintf("%.3f", sapply(pt, `[[`, "lead_re")), "stable"),
    `Cod from above` = above_text(sapply(pt, `[[`, "above_cod_min"),
                                  sapply(pt, `[[`, "above_cod_max")),
    `Sprat from above` = above_text(sapply(sprat_above, min),
                                    sapply(sprat_above, max)),
    check.names = FALSE), align = "lrrlrrrrrrrr")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-departures
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-cap: "Cod biomass after cod are started 20 % below and 20 % above the coexistence state, at the four points of @tbl-points."
dep <- cases$departures
dep$point <- factor(dep$point, levels = pts$label)
# Period of the cycle at the fourth point: the lag beyond 40 years at which
# the last 500 years of the run from above correlate best with themselves
cycling <- dep$cod[dep$point == pts$label[4] & dep$factor > 1 &
                       dep$time > max(dep$time) - 500]
cycle_period <- which.max(acf(cycling, lag.max = 200,
                              plot = FALSE)$acf[-(1:41)]) + 40
dep$start <- factor(ifelse(dep$factor < 1, "20 % below", "20 % above"),
                    levels = c("20 % above", "20 % below"))
ggplot(dep, aes(time, cod, colour = start)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 1, colour = "grey45", linetype = "dashed") +
    geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
    facet_wrap(~point, ncol = 4, labeller = label_wrap_gen(20)) +
    scale_y_log10() +
    coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0.01, 3)) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c("#eb6834", "#2a78d6"),
                        name = "Cod started") +
    labs(x = "Years", y = "Cod biomass / biomass in\nthe coexistence state")
```

@fig-departures shows the runs from below and above at the four points of
@tbl-points:

* **Where the coexistence state is stable**, with or without a barrier, cod
  return to it within about 300 years.
* **Where it is the threshold**, cod started below it die out. Cod started
  above it settle at `r fmt(pt[[2]]$above_cod, 3)` times their coexistence
  biomass at the second point. At the fourth they cycle between
  `r fmt(pt[[4]]$above_cod_min, 2)` and `r fmt(pt[[4]]$above_cod_max, 2)`
  times that biomass, in a pattern that repeats about every
  `r cycle_period` years.

## Decomposition

```{r}
#| label: fig-decomposition
#| fig-height: 5.5
#| fig-cap: "The factors of $R_0$ along the strength of sprat predation on cod larvae, at two strengths of cod predation on sprat (rows). The prey factor and the background factor are above 1 throughout: sprat as food and the background prey work against the Allee effect."
dec <- scan[scan$phi_prey %in% c(0.48, 0.96), ]
factors <- c(prey = "Prey (sprat as food)",
             competition = "Competition (plankton)",
             background = "Background prey",
             larval_predation = "Larval predation",
             R0 = "All together (R0)")
dec_long <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(factors), function(f) {
    data.frame(dec[c("phi_prey", "phi_larv", "variant")],
               factor = factors[[f]], value = dec[[f]])
}))
dec_long$factor <- factor(dec_long$factor, levels = factors)
dec_long$row <- paste("φ_prey =", dec_long$phi_prey)
# Without cod feeding on plankton there is no competition
dec_long <- dec_long[!(dec_long$factor == factors[["competition"]] &
                           dec_long$variant == levels(scan$variant)[1]), ]
ggplot(dec_long, aes(phi_larv, value, colour = factor)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 1, colour = "grey45", linetype = "dashed") +
    geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
    geom_point(size = 1.4) +
    facet_grid(row ~ variant) +
    scale_y_log10() +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c("#eb6834", "#1baf7a", "#8a5cc7", "#2a78d6",
                                   "grey20"), name = NULL) +
    labs(x = "Sprat eating cod larvae, φ_larv",
         y = "R0 of a rare cod in the cod-free state") +
    guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 2))
```

The factors in @fig-decomposition behave very differently:

* **Prey** is `r range_text(on$prey)`: above 1 wherever cod eat sprat. It
  depends on `phi_prey` only. A rare cod in the cod-free state finds more
  adult sprat and grows faster through the sizes of 30 g to 1 kg. As in the
  cultivation–depensation study, food works *against* depensation.
* **Competition** is `r range_text(on$competition[on$cod_resource])` when
  cod larvae eat plankton. It too depends on `phi_prey` only, through the
  number of sprat in the cod-free state.
* **Background** is `r range_text(scan$background)`: above 1 everywhere, and
  largest where cod do not eat sprat at all. A rare cod has to itself the
  background prey that the cod of the coexistence state had eaten down. The
  factor falls as `phi_prey` rises, for two reasons:
  * cod then take more of their food from sprat and less from background
    prey;
  * there are more sprat without cod, and they graze the small background
    prey down, to as little as `r fmt(min(scan$background_free_min), 2)` of
    its abundance in the coexistence state.
* **Food**, all three together, is
  `r range_text(scan$food[!scan$cod_resource])` without competition and
  `r range_text(scan$food[scan$cod_resource])` with it. Food alone closes the
  cod-free state only when cod larvae eat plankton and `phi_prey` is
  `r fmt(min(scan$phi_prey[scan$food < 1]), 2)` or more. At strong links it
  is less than the product of its three parts, because a cod that is already
  well fed gains little from more food.
* **Larval predation** is `r range_text(on$larval_predation[on$phi_larv > 0])`.
  It needs both links: `phi_larv` for sprat to eat cod larvae, and
  `phi_prey` for there to be more sprat without cod.
* **Interaction** is `r range_text(on$interaction[on$cod_resource])` with
  competition and `r range_text(on$interaction[!on$cod_resource])` without.
  Cod larvae short of plankton grow slowly through the sizes at which sprat
  eat them, so competition and larval predation amplify each other. Sprat as
  prey and the background prey hardly interact with larval predation, because
  cod eat them mostly once they have outgrown it.

## Introductions

```{r}
#| label: fig-introductions
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| fig-cap: "Cod biomass after cod are introduced into the cod-free state at a multiple of their abundance in the coexistence state."
intro$point <- factor(intro$point, levels = pts$label)
intro_factors <- sort(unique(intro$factor))
intro$introduced <- factor(paste0(100 * intro$factor, " %"),
                           levels = paste0(100 * intro_factors, " %"))
ggplot(intro, aes(time, cod, colour = introduced)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 1, colour = "grey45", linetype = "dashed") +
    geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
    facet_wrap(~point, ncol = 4, labeller = label_wrap_gen(20)) +
    scale_y_log10(labels = scales::label_log()) +
    coord_cartesian(ylim = c(1e-6, 10)) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c("#b9d6f7", "#6aa5ea", "#2a78d6",
                                   "#0d366b"),
                        name = "Cod introduced (relative to the coexistence state)") +
    labs(x = "Years after introduction",
         y = "Cod biomass / biomass in\nthe coexistence state")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-introductions
#| tbl-cap: "Outcome of the introductions in @fig-introductions after 400 years: cod biomass relative to the coexistence state."
intro_end <- intro[intro$time == max(intro$time), ]
outcome <- biomass_text(intro_end$cod)
outcomes <- sapply(intro_factors, function(f) {
    outcome[intro_end$factor == f][match(pts$label,
                                         intro_end$point[intro_end$factor == f])]
})
colnames(outcomes) <- paste0(100 * intro_factors, " %")
knitr::kable(data.frame(Point = pts$label, outcomes, check.names = FALSE),
             row.names = FALSE)
```

The introductions agree with the regime map (@fig-introductions,
@tbl-introductions):

* **Where there is no barrier** (third point), cod establish from 1 % of
  their coexistence abundance and settle at the coexistence state.
* **Where the coexistence state is stable behind a barrier** (first point),
  1 % and 30 % die out. An introduction at or above the coexistence
  abundance settles at the coexistence state.
* **Where it is the threshold and cod settle above it** (second point), 1 %
  and 30 % die out too. Larger introductions pass the threshold and settle
  above it, with sprat at
  `r fmt(intro_end$sprat[intro_end$point == pts$label[2] & intro_end$factor == 1], 2)`
  of their coexistence biomass.
* **At the fourth point** even three times the coexistence abundance dies
  out.

Note that these introductions go into the cod-free state, where sprat are
more abundant than in the coexistence state. The coexistence abundance of
cod is therefore not itself the threshold.

## Fishing

Cod fishing uses the length-selective trawl of the earlier models, so
$F_\text{cod}$ is the fishing mortality on fully selected cod. Three cod
states are followed, at the first three points of @tbl-points:

* the coexistence state where it is stable behind a barrier;
* where it is the threshold, the state that cod reach from above it. That
  state has `r fmt(up2$Cod[1], 3)` times the cod and
  `r fmt(up2$Sprat[1], 2)` times the sprat of the coexistence state, and no
  longer has power-law rates;
* the coexistence state where there is no barrier.

Each step projects the model until every biomass changes by less than
$10^{-5}$/yr, starting from the state of the previous step. The downward
sweep starts from the cod-free state, with cod topped up to $10^{-6}$ of
their coexistence abundance before each step.

```{r}
#| label: fig-fishing
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-cap: "Equilibrium biomass under increasing (solid, with a point at each step, from the cod state) and decreasing (dashed, from the cod-free state with a cod seed) cod fishing, for the three cod states. Biomasses are relative to the unfished coexistence state. Note the different scales of the fishing mortality. Without a barrier the two sweeps coincide."
# Draw only the branches of steady states, not the jumps between them: each
# sweep is split where cod move between the abundant state and the depleted
# one
settled <- fb[fb$converged, ]
settled$segment <- ave(as.numeric(settled$Cod > abundant),
                       paste(settled$case, settled$sweep),
                       FUN = function(a) cumsum(c(0, diff(a) != 0)))
long <- rbind(transform(settled, species = "Sprat", biomass = Sprat),
              transform(settled, species = "Cod", biomass = Cod))
long$species <- factor(long$species, levels = c("Sprat", "Cod"))
ggplot(long, aes(F_cod, biomass, colour = species)) +
    geom_line(aes(linetype = sweep,
                  group = interaction(species, sweep, segment)),
              linewidth = 0.9) +
    geom_point(data = long[long$sweep == fishing$sweeps[1], ], size = 1.2) +
    facet_wrap(~case, scales = "free_x", labeller = label_wrap_gen(24)) +
    scale_y_continuous(trans = scales::pseudo_log_trans(sigma = 1e-3),
                       breaks = c(0, 1e-3, 1e-2, 0.1, 1),
                       labels = c("0", "0.001", "0.01", "0.1", "1")) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = col_species) +
    labs(x = "Cod fishing mortality F_cod (1/yr)",
         y = "Equilibrium biomass relative to the\nunfished coexistence state (pseudo-log scale)",
         colour = NULL, linetype = NULL) +
    guides(colour = guide_legend(order = 1),
           linetype = guide_legend(order = 2)) +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.box = "vertical")
```

All three cod states withstand very little fishing (@fig-fishing). The cod
state of the combined model persisted up to a fishing mortality of 0.27/yr.

* **The stable coexistence state behind a barrier** persists at
  $F_\text{cod}$ = `r last_F(up1)`/yr, with cod at
  `r fmt(up1$Cod[up1$F_cod == last_F(up1)], 2)` of their unfished biomass, and
  collapses at `r collapse_F(up1)`/yr.
* **The cod state above the threshold** persists at
  $F_\text{cod}$ = `r last_F(up2)`/yr, with cod at
  `r fmt(up2$Cod[up2$F_cod == last_F(up2)], 2)` times their coexistence
  biomass, and collapses at `r collapse_F(up2)`/yr.
* **Cod do not return** in these two cases at any fishing mortality, because
  a rare cod cannot invade the cod-free state
  ($R_0$ = `r fmt(sf1$R0[sf1$F_sprat == 0], 2)` and
  `r fmt(sf2$R0[sf2$F_sprat == 0], 2)`).
* **Without a barrier there is no collapse and no hysteresis.** Cod biomass
  falls steadily, to `r fmt(cod_at(up3, 0.01), 2)` of the unfished biomass at
  $F_\text{cod}$ = 0.01/yr and `r fmt(cod_at(up3, last_F(up3, alive)), 2)` at
  `r last_F(up3, alive)`/yr. Cod are gone at `r collapse_F(up3, alive)`/yr.
  In between, at `r paste(unsettled, collapse = " and ")`/yr, the runs had
  not settled after 3000 years. When fishing is reduced again cod return
  along the same branch: where both sweeps have settled they differ by at
  most `r fmt(sweep_gap, 1)` of the unfished biomass.

**Why so little?** These fishing mortalities are small next to the natural
mortality of cod, which is `r fmt(cod_mort(1000), 2)`/yr at 1 kg and
`r fmt(cod_mort(5000), 2)`/yr at 5 kg. But cod have little to compensate
with:

* Their only density dependence is their food. At a background level of
  `r level` the background prey can at most double when cod become rare.
* That gives a rare cod an $R_0$ of at most `r fmt(max(scan$R0), 3)` in the
  scan, and of `r fmt(sf3$R0[sf3$F_sprat == 0], 3)` at the third point.
  Where there is no barrier, fishing that lowers the lifetime reproduction
  of a cod by that factor removes cod.
* Behind a barrier the cod state is lost earlier, in a fold: it meets the
  threshold while cod are still abundant.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sprat-fishery
#| tbl-cap: "A fishery on sprat above 1 g, without cod fishing, at the first three points of @tbl-points: the invasion fitness of cod in the cod-free state, and cod biomass in the cod state relative to the unfished coexistence state."
sprat_columns <- function(d) {
    d <- d[match(sf1$F_sprat, d$F_sprat), ]
    data.frame(R0 = sprintf("%.2f", d$R0),
               Cod = ifelse(d$cod < alive, "dies out", sprintf("%.2f", d$cod)))
}
sprat_table <- cbind(sf1$F_sprat, sprat_columns(sf1), sprat_columns(sf2),
                     sprat_columns(sf3))
names(sprat_table) <- c("Sprat fishing F (1/yr)",
                        "R0, first point", "Cod, first point",
                        "R0, second point", "Cod, second point",
                        "R0, third point", "Cod, third point")
knitr::kable(sprat_table, align = "rrrrrrr")
```

@vanleeuwen2008 proposed thinning the sprat to let cod recover, and in the
combined model a sprat fishery did open the way back. Here it does too
(@tbl-sprat-fishery):

* **It opens the cod-free state.** Fewer sprat eat fewer cod larvae, leave
  them more plankton and graze less of the small background prey. $R_0$
  exceeds 1 from $F$ = `r min(sf1$F_sprat[sf1$R0 > 1])`/yr at the first
  point and from `r min(sf2$F_sprat[sf2$R0 > 1])`/yr at the second.
* **It also takes the adult sprat that cod eat.** Where cod depend on sprat,
  that lowers cod in the cod state: to
  `r fmt(sf1$cod[sf1$F_sprat == max(sf1$F_sprat)], 2)` of their unfished
  biomass at the first point and
  `r fmt(sf2$cod[sf2$F_sprat == max(sf2$F_sprat)], 2)` at the second, at
  $F$ = `r max(sf1$F_sprat)`/yr.
* **At the third point**, where cod depend least on sprat, cod gain. Their
  biomass is `r fmt(max(sf3$cod), 3)` times the unfished one at
  $F$ = `r sf3$F_sprat[which.max(sf3$cod)]`/yr.

## Sensitivity

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sensitivity
#| tbl-cap: "The second point of @tbl-points with one parameter changed at a time. The last column gives cod biomass, relative to the coexistence state, 1000 years after a start 20 % above it. A range is that of the last 100 years."
sens$unstable <- sens$lead_re > 1e-6
knitr::kable(data.frame(
    Variant = sens$variant,
    `Sprat without cod` = sprintf("%.2f×", sens$sprat_free),
    Prey = sprintf("%.2f", sens$prey),
    Competition = sprintf("%.2f", sens$competition),
    Background = sprintf("%.2f", sens$background),
    `Larval predation` = sprintf("%.2f", sens$larval_predation),
    R0 = sprintf("**%.2f**", sens$R0),
    `Growth rate of the instability (1/yr)` = ifelse(
        sens$unstable, sprintf("%.3f", sens$lead_re), "stable"),
    `Cod from above` = above_text(sens$above_cod_min, sens$above_cod_max),
    check.names = FALSE), align = "lrrrrrrrr")
#' A column of the sensitivity table for one variant
sens_at <- function(variant, column) sens[[column]][sens$variant == variant]
```

@tbl-sensitivity varies what sets how strongly the species and the
background respond, at the second point of @tbl-points:

* **The barrier persists in every variant**, with $R_0$ between
  `r fmt(min(sens$R0), 2)` and `r fmt(max(sens$R0), 2)`. The prey factor
  stays above 1.
* **The background level decides how much of the barrier is left.**
  * The further the background prey gives way, the more a rare cod gains
    from having it to itself. The background factor is
    `r fmt(sens_at("Background level 0.2", "background"), 3)` at a level of
    0.2 and `r fmt(sens_at("Background level 0.8", "background"), 3)` at 0.8.
  * $R_0$ is then `r fmt(sens_at("Background level 0.2", "R0"), 2)` and
    `r fmt(sens_at("Background level 0.8", "R0"), 2)`. With a fixed
    background it is `r fmt(sens_at("Fixed background", "R0"), 2)`.
  * A background prey that gives way more also damps the instability: its
    growth rate is
    `r fmt(sens_at("Background level 0.2", "lead_re"), 2)`/yr at a level of
    0.2 and `r fmt(sens_at("Fixed background", "lead_re"), 2)`/yr with a
    fixed background.
* **The abundance of the background prey** changes neither $R_0$ nor its
  factors. Prey that is ten times as abundant responds ten times as slowly.
  The instability then grows at
  `r fmt(sens_at("Background prey 10 times as abundant", "lead_re"), 2)`/yr
  instead of `r fmt(sens_at("Baseline", "lead_re"), 2)`/yr, and cod started
  above the threshold die out.
* **Plankton that gives way less** (plankton level 0.8) lets sprat increase
  more without cod. Larval predation then matters more and competition
  slightly less.
* **Sprat and cod closer to starvation** (feeding level 0.4) strengthen
  competition, but strengthen the prey factor and the background factor
  against it too. The coexistence state is then stable. Sprat still do not
  become stunted.
* **What happens above the threshold is not robust.** Cod started 20 % above
  it
  * settle above it in most variants;
  * settle below it, with sprat at
    `r fmt(sens_at("Feeding level 0.8", "above_sprat"), 1)` of their
    coexistence biomass (feeding level 0.8);
  * fall to `r fmt(100 * sens_at("Background level 0.2", "above_cod"), 1)` %
    of their coexistence biomass and go on falling slowly (background level
    0.2);
  * or die out (abundant background prey).
* **The numerics do not matter much**: 320 size classes instead of 200 change
  $R_0$ by `r fmt(100 * abs(sens$R0[sens$variant == "320 size classes"] / sens$R0[sens$variant == "Baseline"] - 1), 1)` %.

## Density dependence in cod reproduction

```{r}
#| label: reproduction
bh <- cases$reproduction
bh$stable <- bh$lead_re < 1e-6
bh$barrier <- bh$R0 < 0.999
# The same points without the stock-recruitment relation
bh_scan <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(bh)), function(i) {
    at(bh$phi_prey[i], bh$phi_larv[i], bh$cod_resource[i])
}))
bh$was_stable <- !bh_scan$unstable
bh$was_barrier <- bh_scan$barrier
bh_first <- bh[bh$level == min(bh$level), ]
```

The background prey gives cod a density dependence through their food. The
mizerEcopath workflow normally ends by giving each species one in its
reproduction as well: a Beverton–Holt stock–recruitment relation with a
chosen reproduction level $L$, the ratio of recruitment to its maximum. That
was tried for cod at `r nrow(bh_first)` points of the scan (`phi_prey` 0.48
and 0.96, `phi_larv` 0.24 and 0.72, with and without cod larvae eating
plankton), each with $L$ = 0.5 and 0.8. Without it the coexistence state is
stable at `r sum(bh_first$was_stable)` of these points, and
`r sum(bh_first$was_barrier)` have a barrier. It does not widen the
bistability:

* **It does not stabilise the coexistence state.** At all
  `r sum(!bh_first$was_stable)` points where the state is unstable it stays
  unstable for both values of $L$. The instability only grows more slowly.
* **It weakens the barrier.** To keep the coexistence state a steady state,
  `erepro` rises by a factor $1/(1-L)$, and with it $R_0$ at low density. The
  cod-free state stays closed only where $R_0$ was below $1 - L$: in
  `r sum(bh$barrier)` of the `r nrow(bh)` runs.
* **Never both.** In all `r sum(bh$barrier)` runs with a barrier the
  coexistence state is unstable, and in all `r sum(bh$stable)` runs where it
  is stable cod invade the cod-free state. The point that is bistable
  without the relation (`phi_prey` = 0.96, `phi_larv` = 0.24, cod larvae
  eating background food only) loses its barrier.

A stable coexistence state needs the density dependence at that state to
outweigh the positive feedback there. A closed cod-free state needs the
positive feedback, summed from no cod up to the coexistence abundance, to
outweigh $1/(1-L)$. Both hold only if the positive feedback is much stronger
at low cod abundance than at the coexistence abundance. Here it is not.

# Comparison with the combined model

| | [Combined model](combined_model.html) | This model |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Community | Cod, sprat, plankton | The same, in a power-law background of fixed mortality and depletable prey |
| Cod state | Held fixed by recalibrating `erepro` | The same steady state for all link strengths, by construction |
| Sprat as food for cod | Barrier (the mechanism of Van Leeuwen et al.) for early diet shifts | Never a barrier: raises $R_0$ |
| Sprat eating cod larvae | Barrier | Barrier, down to a factor `r fmt(min(scan$larval_predation), 2)` |
| Competition for plankton | Excluded | Optional. A barrier when included |
| Other food of cod | None | Background prey that cod eat down. Works against the barriers |
| The two barriers together | Amplify each other | Larval predation and competition amplify each other. Sprat as food does not interact |
| Cod state | Stable up to moderate larval predation | Stable wherever cod can invade. Behind a barrier mostly the threshold, with a cod state above it |
| Cod fishing | The cod state persists up to 0.27/yr | The cod states behind a barrier collapse at `r collapse_F(up1)`/yr and `r collapse_F(up2)`/yr |
| Sprat fishery | Opens the way back | Opens the way back |
| Numerics | Second order, size diffusion | First-order upwind |

# Caveats

* **The background responds only in part.**
  * Its mortality is fixed: the other predators of cod and sprat do not
    change in number or switch prey.
  * Background prey below 0.1 g is fixed. With cod larvae eating background
    food only, their food is therefore fixed.
  * The background prey has no dynamics of its own beyond the semichemostat:
    its size classes do not grow into each other or feed on the plankton.
* **Two numbers for the background prey are free choices.**
  * The background level sets how far the prey gives way. At 1 the
    background is fixed.
  * The abundance of the prey sets how fast it gives way, but not how far.
    It changes the eigenvalues and the transients, and leaves the steady
    states and $R_0$ as they are. @tbl-sensitivity varies both.
* **Cod can compensate for little.** Their food is their only density
  dependence, and it gives a rare cod an $R_0$ of at most
  `r fmt(max(scan$R0), 3)`. That is why so little fishing removes them
  (@fig-fishing). The fishing mortalities here should not be read as
  estimates for a real stock.
* **One number scales each link.** The size pattern of each link (@fig-shares)
  follows from the kernels and the spectra and is not a free choice. Small
  cod cannot be made to depend on small sprat without a kernel that changes
  with size.
* **One biomass ratio.** The biomasses of cod and sprat are those of the
  [cod–sprat model](index.html). Their ratio decides how much sprat
  mortality cod can account for when cod depend fully on sprat.
* **Sprat respond weakly to food.** With a feeding level of 0.6, a critical
  level of 0.2 and plankton at half its capacity, sprat cannot become
  stunted. @tbl-sensitivity varies these.
* **Stability.**
  * `getStability()` returns a ladder of real eigenvalues between about
    $-10^{-3}$/yr and rounding error, from sizes of plankton and background
    prey that no fish eats.
    They hide how strongly a stable state is damped, so only instability is
    read from the eigenvalues.
  * The fate of cod above the threshold comes from one projection, started
    with cod 20 % above the coexistence state and everything else
    unchanged, and judged after 1000 years. Such a start need not lie in the
    basin of a cod state above the threshold. Cycles were not characterised.
  * Large background prey responds slowly, because only the few large cod
    eat it: prey of 5 kg is replenished at
    `r fmt(at_prey(resource_rate(p_max), 5000), 1)`/yr. Transients therefore
    take centuries.
* **Numerics.** First-order upwind on 200 size classes, with its numerical
  diffusion. With 320 classes $R_0$ at the second point of @tbl-points
  changes by `r fmt(100 * abs(sens$R0[sens$variant == "320 size classes"] / sens$R0[sens$variant == "Baseline"] - 1), 1)` %.
* **Internals.** `cod_R0()` calls mizer internals and was written against
  mizer 3.4.0.9001. The results here were computed with mizer
  `r res$mizer_version` and mizerEcopath `r res$mizerEcopath_version`.

# Possible next steps

* A background mortality that responds: other predators that switch to cod
  or sprat when those are abundant.
* A background level chosen from data on how far cod deplete their other
  prey.
* More compensation in cod, so that the cod states withstand a realistic
  fishing mortality. A lower background level and density dependence in cod
  reproduction both give that, and both weaken the barriers.
* A diet of cod that shifts with size, so that small cod can depend on small
  sprat and the mechanism of @vanleeuwen2008 gets a fair chance in a
  power-law community.
* Sprat that are closer to starvation in the coexistence state (a lower
  feeding level for sprat only), so that they can become stunted.
* The fishing thresholds across the regime map, and a sprat fishery as a way
  back from the cod-free state.

# Reproducing this document

| File | Contents |
|:--|:--|
| `R/background_model.R` | The model, the cod-free state, the stability measures and the decomposition of $R_0$ |
| `background/run_scan.R` | The scan over the two links; writes `background/scan.rds` |
| `background/run_cases.R` | Spectra, runs from below and above the coexistence state, introductions, sensitivity and density-dependent reproduction at single points; writes `background/cases.rds` |
| `background/run_fishing.R` | The branches under cod fishing and the effect of a sprat fishery; writes `background/fishing.rds` |
| `background_model.qmd` | This document; it reads the three results files |

```bash
OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1 OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 Rscript background/run_scan.R
OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1 OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 Rscript background/run_cases.R
OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1 OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 Rscript background/run_fishing.R
quarto render background_model.qmd
```

The scan takes about an hour and a half on 4 cores, and the other two scripts
about 35 and 20 minutes.
The model needs the mizerEcopath package, which brings in mizerFromEcopath.

This document was rendered with mizer `r packageVersion("mizer")`,
mizerEcopath `r packageVersion("mizerEcopath")` and `r R.version.string`.
